passage: Class teacher's note, Class 6. During today's Independence Day rehearsal, the flag went up and the anthem began. Madhav stood straight, arms at his sides, eyes on the flag. Beside him, Dhruv was poking the boy in front. Madhav said nothing during the anthem, but afterwards he told Dhruv, "My Dadaji says the anthem is 52 seconds. We can stand still that long." Dhruv shrugged, but in the second run-through he stood still. Madhav also offered to help the school helper fold the flag properly. I will ask him to lead the flag-folding team on the day.

qa.q: How long did Madhav say the anthem lasts?
qa.a: 52 seconds.

qa.q: Why did Madhav wait until after the anthem to speak to Dhruv?
qa.a: He respected the anthem too much to talk during it, and wanted to remind Dhruv without making a scene.

qa.q: Why is asking Madhav to lead the flag-folding team a good idea?
qa.a: It gives his respect for the flag a real role and lets him show others how to do it properly.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel after Madhav's comment?
qa.a: Maybe a little annoyed, but he stood still the second time, which suggests it made sense to him.

grounding: It shows, in a teacher's note, a boy honouring the flag and anthem and encouraging a classmate to do the same.

passage:
Diary, Thursday.
Our class visited the district court today. I thought it would be boring, but when the judge came in and everyone stood, I got goosebumps. Our guide said the building is 120 years old and belongs to all of us, so no scribbling on the benches. Vaibhav from my class tried to put his feet up in the waiting hall, and the guard told him off. I felt embarrassed for our school. At home I told Nanaji about it. He said that when he first voted, he wore his best shirt. I want to feel like that when I vote too.
- Madhuri

qa.q: How old is the court building, according to the guide?
qa.a: 120 years old.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri feel embarrassed when Vaibhav put his feet up?
qa.a: Madhuri felt the building deserved respect and that his behaviour reflected badly on their school.

qa.q: How could the teacher build on this visit?
qa.a: Ask the class to discuss why public buildings and institutions belong to everyone, and how to show respect in them.

qa.q: What does Nanaji's best-shirt story suggest about how he sees voting?
qa.a: He sees it as an important, proud moment worth dressing up for.

grounding: It shows a child feeling respect for a public institution and valuing an elder's civic pride.

passage: On Republic Day, rain had turned the village school ground into mud, but the whole village came anyway. Eshaan and Aadhya, both ten, had been chosen to carry the folded flag to the pole. Eshaan held it flat on his palms, wrapped in a plastic sheet so no drop would touch it. Aadhya walked beside him with an umbrella tilted over the flag, not over herself. When the sarpanch pulled the rope and the petals fell, Eshaan's grandfather, an old postman, saluted from under a sack. Afterwards Aadhya said, "My shoulders are soaked, but the flag is dry."

qa.q: What did Eshaan wrap the flag in?
qa.a: A plastic sheet.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya hold the umbrella over the flag and not herself?
qa.a: She cared about keeping the flag dry and respected, even more than keeping herself dry.

qa.q: How could the teacher recognise what the two children did?
qa.a: Thank them in front of the school for how carefully they carried the flag, so others see what respect looks like.

qa.q: How might Eshaan's grandfather feel watching his grandson carry the flag?
qa.a: Proud and moved, which may be why he saluted even from under a sack in the rain.

grounding: It shows village children honouring the national flag with care during a rainy Republic Day.

passage: On Monday mornings at their school in Cape Town, the flag went up while the anthem played through a crackly speaker. Thabo, ten, took off his cap and stood still, even though his shoelace was undone. Yara, who had arrived from Jordan in March, whispered, 'Why does everyone go so quiet?' Thabo waited for the last note. 'My gogo says it's for everyone who worked to make this country fair,' he whispered back. 'She was there when it changed.' Yara thought about it. At lunch she drew her own country's flag in her notebook and showed him. Thabo studied it carefully. 'Teach me what the colours mean,' he said, 'and I'll teach you the words of ours.'

qa.q: Where was Thabo's school?
qa.a: It was in Cape Town.

qa.q: Why did Thabo stand still even with his shoelace undone?
qa.a: He felt the anthem deserved his respect, partly because his gogo connected it with people who worked to make the country fair.

qa.q: How could a teacher build on the swap Thabo suggested?
qa.a: A teacher could invite children to share the flags and songs of their families' countries, so respect for symbols includes everyone's.

qa.q: What might the flag moment feel like for Yara as a newcomer?
qa.a: It may have felt confusing at first, then more welcoming once Thabo explained and asked about her own flag. 🤍

grounding: Shows a child honouring the national flag and anthem, linked to a grandparent's story, and respecting a classmate's flag too.

passage: The day before Republic Day, the scouts' room smelled of starch and marigolds. Arohi, twelve, and Gurpreet had been chosen to fold the flag so it would open cleanly at the ceremony. Gurpreet swung one corner round his shoulders like a cape. 'Superhero!' Arohi caught the cloth before it brushed the floor. 'Not on the ground. Sir said.' 'It's just practice.' 'Still.' She showed him how the petals go inside the last fold, the way the scout teacher had shown them, slowly, twice. Gurpreet stopped fooling and copied her. When the teacher checked, the bundle held. 'Good,' he said. 'Who noticed it nearly touched the floor?' Gurpreet, a little red, pointed at Arohi. 'She did.'

qa.q: What was placed inside the last fold?
qa.a: Petals were placed inside the last fold.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel when she caught the cloth so quickly?
qa.a: She felt protective of the flag and alarmed that it might touch the floor, since the teacher had said it must stay off the ground.

qa.q: What made Arohi's correction work?
qa.a: She did not scold; she showed him the proper fold slowly, which gave him a way to join in.

qa.q: What might Gurpreet have felt when he pointed at Arohi?
qa.a: Probably a bit embarrassed about his joke, but honest enough to give her the credit.

grounding: Illustrates a child treating the national flag with respect during a school ceremony rehearsal and following the school's rule.

passage: I'm Raghav, Zubin's classmate. At our school's Independence Day assembly, when the anthem started, most of us were shuffling or whispering. Zubin, who's eleven, stood completely still, chin up, hands at his sides. After the anthem, the wind blew one of the small paper flags off the stage. Zubin walked over, picked it up, dusted it off and handed it back to the teacher. Some boys laughed. He didn't seem to care. I don't know what he was feeling, but he looked proud.

qa.q: What did Zubin pick up after the anthem?
qa.a: One of the small paper flags.

qa.q: What might Zubin have been feeling during the anthem?
qa.a: He seemed proud and respectful, taking the moment seriously.

qa.q: How could the teacher respond to Zubin picking up the flag?
qa.a: Thank him quietly and use it to remind the class why the flag is treated with respect.

qa.q: How might Raghav see Zubin after the boys laughed?
qa.a: Raghav seems a bit impressed that Zubin didn't care about the laughter.

grounding: Shows a child honouring the anthem and flag at a school assembly, seen by a classmate.

passage: Two weeks before Republic Day: Gopika, ten, was bored at parade practice. "Why do we march for a day off?" she asked her brother Karthik. One week before: her teacher read the Preamble aloud and explained that it was a promise to every citizen. Gopika copied it neatly into her notebook. Republic Day: she marched in the front row, arms swinging. That afternoon she stuck the Preamble on the fridge and read it to Karthik, who rolled his eyes but listened.

qa.q: What did Gopika stick on the fridge?
qa.a: The Preamble.

qa.q: How did Gopika's feelings about Republic Day change?
qa.a: She went from bored to proud once she understood what the Preamble promised.

qa.q: What helped Gopika's attitude change?
qa.a: Her teacher explaining the meaning behind the day, not just the marching.

qa.q: What is it like for Karthik when Gopika reads the Preamble to him?
qa.a: He acts bored but listens, maybe a bit curious about his sister's new pride.

grounding: Shows a child moving from boredom to respect for a national day as she learns its meaning.

passage: "Hemant, you ask why I always fold the flag carefully. When I, your Nilesh Dada, was ten, our village school got its first proper flagpole. On Independence Day the headmaster chose me to pull the rope. I was so nervous that the flag got stuck halfway. Everyone was watching. My ears were burning. The headmaster walked over, calmly untangled it, and let me finish. Afterwards he showed me how to fold it, corner to corner, and said, 'We don't just own this. We look after it.' I've never forgotten."

qa.q: What did the headmaster choose Nilesh to do?
qa.a: To pull the rope.

qa.q: How did young Nilesh feel when the flag got stuck halfway?
qa.a: He felt nervous and embarrassed, with everyone watching.

qa.q: What turning point in the story shaped Nilesh's respect for the flag?
qa.a: The headmaster calmly helping him finish and then teaching him to fold it carefully.

qa.q: How might the headmaster have seen the stuck flag?
qa.a: As a chance to teach respect and care rather than as a failure.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a child he learned to honour the flag and school ceremonies.

passage: It was pouring on Independence Day in Coimbatore, but the school still held the flag hoisting. The students stood in the ground, raincoats dripping. Lavanya's shoe was full of water. As the flag went up and the anthem began, she stood straight, hands at her sides, and sang every word. Next to her, Disha was giggling and shaking rain off her plait. Lavanya glanced at her, then back at the flag. After the anthem Disha said, "Weren't you freezing?" "Yes," Lavanya said. "But it's our anthem." Disha stopped giggling.

qa.q: What was full of water?
qa.a: Lavanya's shoe.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling when she stood straight in the rain?
qa.a: She felt respectful and proud of the anthem, even while cold and wet.

qa.q: How could a teacher recognise the students who stood still in the rain?
qa.a: A teacher could thank them afterwards for respecting the ceremony despite the weather.

qa.q: How might Disha see Lavanya's answer?
qa.a: Disha seemed to feel a little embarrassed, stopping her giggling after Lavanya's reply.

grounding: A girl stands still for the anthem on a rainy Independence Day, showing respect for the flag.

passage: The day after Republic Day, the lane in Vashi was littered with small paper flags. Nikita, ten, stopped on the way to school and picked one up from a puddle. She shook it dry and held it carefully. Her mother, Nirmala, looked at her. "Why that one?" "It's the flag, Mumma. It shouldn't be on the road." At home she flattened it under a heavy book, then folded it into her drawer. That evening, she told her grandmother about the flags in the lane. "I'll pick up more tomorrow," Nikita said.

qa.q: Where did Nikita pick up the flag from?
qa.a: From a puddle.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when she saw the flags in the lane?
qa.a: She felt concerned and respectful, uncomfortable seeing the flag lying on the road.

qa.q: How could Nirmala support Nikita's plan to pick up more flags?
qa.a: She could go with her and help collect the flags safely before school.

qa.q: How might Nikita's grandmother react when she hears about the flags?
qa.a: She might feel proud of Nikita's respect for the national flag.

grounding: A girl picks up a discarded paper flag from a puddle after Republic Day out of respect.

passage:
"Farida Phuphi, why are we standing in this line so long?"
"Because we're at the post office, Rafiq. Everyone waits their turn."
"But you know the man at the counter. Just go to the front."
"And if everyone who knew him did that?"
Rafiq thought. "Then the line would never move."
"Exactly. This office sends letters for the whole town. Your Dadi's pension, your cousin's forms. If it's unfair, people stop trusting it."
Rafiq shuffled forward. "It's still boring."
"Very boring," Phuphi agreed. "But we wait."

qa.q: Where were Rafiq and Farida Phuphi standing in line?
qa.a: At the post office.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when he suggested going to the front?
qa.a: He felt bored and impatient with the long wait.

qa.q: What did Farida Phuphi's question help Rafiq understand?
qa.a: That skipping the queue is unfair to others and can harm trust in the post office.

qa.q: How might the other people in line feel if someone skipped ahead?
qa.a: They would likely feel annoyed and treated unfairly.

grounding: An aunt explains to a boy why they wait their turn at the post office, respecting a public institution.

passage:
On Independence Day when I was nine, our school lined up in the ground for the flag hoisting. It was drizzling.

When the anthem began, Jasleen, next to me, started giggling at a boy who'd slipped in the mud. I wanted to laugh too.

But I remembered my Dadaji, who had been in the army. He always stood very still for the anthem, even at home when it played on television.

So I stood still, hands at my sides, until the last note. Afterwards, Jasleen said, "You're so serious." I said, "Only for fifty-two seconds."

I'm Irawati, and I still stand still.

qa.q: What made Jasleen giggle?
qa.a: A boy who'd slipped in the mud.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel during the anthem?
qa.a: Irawati felt tempted to laugh but respectful and proud, remembering Dadaji.

qa.q: What helped Irawati show respect for the anthem?
qa.a: Remembering how Dadaji always stood still helped.

qa.q: How might Jasleen see Irawati's seriousness?
qa.a: Jasleen found it a bit too serious, but may have been curious about it.

grounding: A child remembers standing still for the national anthem at a rainy Independence Day event.

passage:
Teacher's note, Republic Day rehearsal, January.

Deepika, eleven, was on flag duty. She checked twice that the flag was folded correctly with the flowers inside. When another student dropped the rope on the ground, she picked it up and dusted it without being asked.

She also reminded her group, quietly, to stand straight during the anthem. They did.

After the event, she helped fold the flag again. I've asked her to teach the next flag team. — Noor

qa.q: What did Deepika check twice?
qa.a: She checked that the flag was folded correctly with the flowers inside.

qa.q: How might Deepika have felt on flag duty?
qa.a: Deepika likely felt proud and responsible, taking the duty seriously.

qa.q: How did Noor recognise Deepika's respect?
qa.a: Noor asked Deepika to teach the next flag team.

qa.q: How might Deepika's group feel when she reminded them?
qa.a: They might feel encouraged to stand straight, following her example.

grounding: A teacher notes a girl showing respect for the national flag and rules at a Republic Day rehearsal.

passage:
Gandhi Jayanti, Monday

Went with Sarita Bua to the post office today. Dadi's pension letter had come and needed signing.

The post office was crowded and hot. A man pushed to the front shouting. The clerk asked him politely to wait his turn.

Bua waited forty minutes. She said, "The post office brings Dadi's pension every month. They work hard. We should be patient." When our turn came, she said thank you to the clerk twice.

On the way out, I saw Gandhiji's picture on the wall.

Sunaina

qa.q: How long did Sarita Bua wait?
qa.a: Bua waited forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel watching Bua thank the clerk?
qa.a: Sunaina probably felt respectful and curious, noticing how Bua valued the post office.

qa.q: What could Sunaina learn from Bua about respecting institutions?
qa.a: To be patient, follow the queue, and thank workers who serve the public.

qa.q: How might the clerk feel when Bua thanked him?
qa.a: The clerk might feel appreciated after a hot, busy day.

grounding: On Gandhi Jayanti, a child learns respect for a public institution from an aunt at the post office.

passage: On Republic Day the village school in Kottayam district held its flag-hoisting in a light January drizzle. Alka had ironed her white uniform the night before and polished her shoes by lamplight. When the panchayat president pulled the cord and petals fell from the flag, the anthem began. Alka stood straight, eyes on the flag. Beside her, Joseph shuffled and whispered about the sweets after. Alka didn't turn, but pressed her elbow lightly against his. He went still. Later, when the old postmaster, who had worked there forty years, was given a shawl, Alka clapped the loudest. "He brought Appachan's letters from the Gulf for years," she told Joseph.

qa.q: Who pulled the cord to hoist the flag?
qa.a: The panchayat president pulled the cord.

qa.q: Why did Alka clap loudest for the old postmaster?
qa.a: She felt grateful and admiring, remembering that he carried her Appachan's letters for years.

qa.q: How did Alka handle Joseph's whispering, and why did it work?
qa.a: A light nudge without turning kept the anthem respectful without embarrassing Joseph in front of everyone.

qa.q: How might Joseph see the ceremony after Alka's explanation?
qa.a: Joseph may start to see the postmaster and the day as more than sweets, since Alka linked it to her family's life.

grounding: Shows a child honouring the flag and anthem and valuing a long-serving public servant on Republic Day.
